d.x: ...the supposed Extraversion or Intraversion of Sulphur...

extraversion.e: From New Latin extrāversio, from Classical Latin extrā- (“outside”) + versio (“a turning”). Equivalent to extravert + -sion. Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung.

d.g: The degree or property of being extreme.

extremeness.e: English extreme Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English extremeness From extreme + -ness.

d.g: Extreme ideas or actions, primarily in politics or religion.
d.x: For a student of American history and a foreigner like myself, it is easier to understand all these extremisms of conscience.

extremism.e: English extreme Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. d.g: The most extreme or furthest point of something.
d.x: [B]eſtowe your love on him, who, were it not to do you ſervice, would through the extremitie of love rather wiſh to die then live.

d.g: An extreme measure.
A hand or foot.
d.x: Guillain–Barré syndrome causes one to not be able to move one’s extremities.

d.g: A limb (“major appendage of a human or animal such as an arm, leg, or wing”).
d.x: The danger of wounds of the extremities consists in the injury done to the blood-vessels, nerves, articulations, and bones.

extremity.e: From Middle English extremite, from Old French extremité, from Latin extrēmitātem (“extremity; border, perimeter; ending”), from extrēmīs (“furthest, extreme”) + -itās (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being); see extreme. …

d.g: A point, or value that is a maximum or a minimum.

extremum.e: Learned borrowing from Latin extrēmum, neuter form of extrēmus (“extreme in degree”). Doublet of extreme.

d.g: The act or process of extricating or disentangling; a freeing from perplexities; disentanglement.
Rescue of a trapped person in a vehicle or machinery.
The act of sending out or evolving.

extrication.e: English extricate Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English -ion English extrication From extricate + -ion.

d.g: Negentropy.

d.g: The condition of being inside out, especially in relation to the bladder.
d.x: In extroversion of the bladder the anterior part of this organ is more or less completely wanting.

d.g: A personality orientation towards others and things outside oneself; behavior expressing such orientation.
d.x: Extroversion is the thrusting out of the mind on to life, the use of the mind in practical affairs, the pouring out of the libido on external objects.

extroversion.e: From extro- + -version. As a variant of extraversion, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's use of the (then nonstandard) spelling extrovert in her publication "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte" (1918).

d.g: A manufacturing process where a billet of material is pushed and/or drawn through a die to create a shaped rod, rail or pipe.
An item formed by the process of extrusion.

extrusion.e: Mid-16th century from Latin extrūdere, from ex- (“out”) + trūdere (“to thrust”).

d.g: The quality of being exuberant; cheerful or vigorous enthusiasm; liveliness.
d.x: Tottenham's desire for a win against a Norwich side playing with energy and exuberance made for an enthralling, end-to-end game.

d.g: An instance of exuberant behaviour.
An overflowing quantity; superfluousness.
d.x: an exuberance of branches in a plant

d.g: An abundance of wealth.

exuberance.e: From French exubérance, from Latin exuberantia (“superabundance”), from exuberare (“to grow thickly, to abound”); from ex- (“out”) + uber (“udder”), which would have originally referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

d.g: A fluid that has exuded from somewhere; especially one that has exuded from a pore of an animal or plant.
d.x: The whitish lines of exudate seem at times to penetrate even between the straight tubes . . .

exudate.e: English exude English -ate English exudate From exude + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

d.g: The act or process of exuding.
d.x: In severe burns, the body loses large amounts of nitrogen, in the urine and by exudation from the burned body surface.

d.g: Something that is exuded.
d.x: The skin must be frequently and thoroughly washed, occasionally with warm water and soap, to remove the oily exudations upon its surface.

exudation.e: English exude Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English exudation From exude + -ation.

d.g: The act of exulting; great joy at success or victory, or at any advantage gained; rapturous delight
A group of skylarks; the collective noun for skylarks.

exultation.e: From Middle English exultacion, from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, exsultātiōnem.

d.g: A residential area beyond the suburbs.

exurbia.e: English exurb Latin -iader. English -ia English exurbia From exurb + -ia.

d.g: plural of exuvia
The coverings of an animal that have been shed or cast off, particularly the molted exoskeletons of arthropods.
Among the Ancient Romans, weaponry and equipment stripped from the person of a foe; booty.

exuviae.e: Learned borrowing from Latin exuviae, from exuō (“cast off, undress”).

d.g: To make worse (a problem, bad situation, negative feeling, etc.).
d.x: Near-synonym: worsen

exacerbate.e: First attested in 1660; borrowed from Latin exacerbātus, perfect passive participle of Latin exacerbō (“to provoke”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out of; thoroughly”) + acerbō (“to embitter, harshen or worsen”).

d.g: To overstate, to describe more than the fact.
d.x: I've told you a billion times not to exaggerate!

d.g: Exaggerative; overblown.
d.x: And in general, if it is a natural feeling, let it be, but at normal, living levels, not too exaggerate.

exaggerate.e: Borrowed from Latin exaggerātus, perfect passive participle of exaggerō (“to heap up, increase, enlarge, magnify, amplify, exaggerate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out, up”) + aggerō, aggerāre (“to heap up”), from agger (“a pile, heap, mound, dike, mole, pier, etc.”) …

d.g: To honor; to hold in high esteem; to praise or worship.
d.x: The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high.

d.g: To raise in rank, status etc., to elevate.
d.x: The man was exalted from a humble carpenter to a minister.

d.g: To elate, or fill with the joy of success.

exalt.e: From Middle English exalten, from Old French exalter, from Latin exaltō.

d.g: To observe carefully or critically to learn about someone or something.
d.x: He examined the crime scene for clues.

d.g: To check the health or condition of something or someone.
d.x: The doctor examined the patient.

d.g: To determine the aptitude, skills or qualifications of someone by subjecting them to an examination.
To interrogate.
d.x: The witness was examined under oath.

d.g: An act of examining.
d.x: Soutar scratched the back of his neck then had a quick examine of his nails. Deep-ingrained purple they were.

examine.e: From Middle English examinen, examenen, from Old French examiner, from Latin exāmināre.

d.g: To tax the patience of; irk, frustrate, vex, provoke, annoy; to make angry.
d.x:
And this report
Hath so exasperate [sic] the king that he
Prepares for some attempt of war.

d.g: To overaspirate the letter h, or to aspirate it whenever it begins a word, once a common form of hypercorrection.
d.x:
quoted (from Punch magazine) in 2005, David Crystal, The Stories of English
COCKNEY HOBSERVATION. — Cockneys are not the only people who drop or exasperate the 'h's.' It is done by common people in the provinces, and you may laugh at them for it.

exasperate.e: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin exasperātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin exasperō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out of; thoroughly”) + asperō (“to make rough”), from asper (“rough”). …

d.g: To make a hole in (something); to hollow.
To remove part of (something) by scooping or digging it out.
To uncover (something) by digging.
Made hollow.

excavate.e: First attested in 1599, from Latin excavātus (“hollowed out”), perfect passive participle of excavō (“to hollow out”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out”) + cavō (“to hollow out, pierce”), from cavus (“cave, hole”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). …

d.g: To be larger, greater than (something).
d.x: The company's 2005 revenue exceeds that of 2004.

d.g: To be better than (something).
d.x: The quality of her essay has exceeded my expectations.

d.g: To go beyond (some limit); to surpass; to be longer than.
d.x: Your password cannot exceed eight characters.

d.g: To predominate.

exceed.e: From Middle English exceden, from Old French exceder, from Latin excēdō (“to go beyond”), from ex- (“out, forth”) with cēdō (“to go”); see cede and compare accede etc. Partly displaced native Old English ofersteppan, whence Modern English overstep.

d.g: To surpass someone or something; to be better or do better than someone or something.
d.x: I excelled everyone else with my exam results.

d.g: To be much better than others.
d.x: But it is as a destroyer of grasshoppers that the dickcissel excels.

d.g: To exceed, to go beyond.
d.x: She opened; but to shut / Excelled her power: the gates wide open stood […]

excel.e: From Middle English excellen, from Old French exceller, from Latin excellere, excelsum; ex (“out”) + *cellō, an unattested verb root found in culmen (“height, top”); Compare French exceller. See also culminate, column.

d.g: To exclude; to specify as being an exception.
d.x: I find most people annoying — present company excepted, of course!

d.g: To take exception, to object (to or against).
d.x: to except to a witness or his testimony

d.g: Used to introduce an exception or qualification to something previously stated.
d.x: There was nothing in the cupboard except a tin of beans.

d.g: Used to introduce a clause, phrase, verb infinitive, adverb or other non-noun complement forming an exception or qualification to something previously stated.
d.x: You look a bit like my sister, except (that) she has longer hair.

d.g: Loosely, used to introduce a contrastive statement explaining why something wasn't successful, didn't happen, etc.
d.x: They fired tear gas at us, except the wind was blowing the wrong way.

d.g: take exception to

except.e: Borrowed from Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus.

d.g: To stir the emotions of; to cause to feel excitement.
d.x: The fireworks which opened the festivities excited anyone present.

d.g: To arouse or bring out (e.g. feelings); to stimulate.
d.x: Favoritism tends to excite jealousy in the ones not being favored.

d.g: To cause an electron to move to a higher than normal state; to promote an electron to an outer level.
d.x: By applying electric potential to the neon atoms, the electrons become excited, then emit a photon when returning to normal.

d.g: To energize (an electromagnet); to produce a magnetic field in.
d.x: to excite a dynamo

excite.e: From Middle English exciten, from Old French exciter, from Latin excitō (“to call out, call forth, arouse, wake up, stimulate”), frequentative of excieō (“to call out, arouse, excite”), from ex (“out”) + cieō (“to call, summon”). See cite and compare to accite, concite, incite.

d.g: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.
d.x:
I am a soldier, and unapt to weep,
Or to exclaim on fortune’s fickleness.

d.g: To say suddenly and with strong emotion.
d.x: […] her aunt, after having stared at me a good while with a look of amazement, exclaimed, “In the name of heaven! Who art thou?”—

exclaim.e: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).

d.g: To bar (someone or something) from entering; to keep out.
To expel; to put out.
d.x: to exclude young animals from the womb or from eggs

d.g: To omit from consideration.
d.x: Count from 1 to 30, but exclude the prime numbers.

d.g: To refuse to accept (evidence) as valid.

exclude.e: Borrowed from Latin exclūdō, from prefix ex- (“out”) + variant form of verb claudō (“close”).

d.g: To think over something carefully; to consider fully; cogitate.
d.x: Did he ponder the harmony of the spheres? Certainly not: celestial spheres were first excogitated decades or more after Pythagoras' death.

d.g: To reach as a conclusion through reason or careful thought.
d.x: After many years of study, he excogitated a solution.

excogitate.e: From Latin excōgitāre, from ex- + cōgitāre (“think”).

d.g: To officially exclude someone from membership of a church or religious community.
To exclude from any other group; to banish.
d.x: Although our Macs served us well, in those early, dark years Macintosh users were effectively excommunicated by the computer establishment.

d.g: An excommunicated person.

excommunicate.e: From Ecclesiastical Latin excommunicātus, perfect passive participle of excommunicō (“excommunicate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ex- + communicate.

d.g: to remove the skin and/or fur of, to flay, to skin
To wear off the skin of; to chafe.
To strongly condemn or criticize.
d.x: The teacher continued to excoriate the student after his academic issues.

excoriate.e: First attested in the first part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English *excoriaten (only attested in its past participle), borrowed from Late Latin excoriātus perfect passive participle of excoriō (“to take the skin or hide off, flay, skin”), from ex- (“out off, from”) + corium (“hide, s …

d.g: To discharge material (including waste products) from a cell, body or system.
d.x: Your open pores excrete sweat and dirt.

excrete.e: Borrowed from Latin excrētum, past participle of excernō, from ex- (“out”), and cernō (“separate”).

d.g: To inflict intense pain or mental distress on (someone); to torture.

excruciate.e: From Latin excruciātus, past participle of excruciō, from ex- + cruciō, from the base of crux (“cross”).

d.g: To clear of or to free from guilt; exonerate.

exculpate.e: From Medieval Latin exculpātus, perfect passive participle of exculpō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out, from”) + culpa (“fault; blame”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To feel loathing for; to abhor.
d.x: Yet she appeared confident in innocence, and did not tremble, although gazed on and execrated by thousands ; […]

d.g: To declare to be hateful or abhorrent; to denounce.

execrate.e: From Latin exsecrārī, execrārī, from ex (“out”) + sacrāre (“to consecrate, declare accursed”).

d.g: To kill, especially as punishment for a capital crime.
d.x: There are certain states where it is lawful to execute prisoners convicted of certain crimes.

d.g: To carry out; to put into effect.
d.x: Your orders have been executed, sir!

d.g: To perform.
d.x: to execute a difficult piece of music brilliantly

d.g: To carry out, to perform an act; to put into effect or cause to become legally binding or valid (as a contract) by so doing.
d.x: to execute a contract

execute.e: From Old French executer (French exécuter), from Latin exsecutus, past participle of exsequor (“to follow (up/through)”, particularly in the sense “to go through with a deed or punishment”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”).

d.g: To show or illustrate by example.
To be an instance of or serve as an example.
To make an attested copy or transcript of (a document) under seal.
To prove by such an attested copy or transcript.

exemplify.e: From Medieval Latin exemplificare, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

d.g: To disembowel; to eviscerate.

exenterate.e: Learned borrowing from Latin exenterātus, perfect passive participle of exenterō (“to disembowel”). First attested in 1607.

d.g: To make use of, to apply, especially of something non-material; to bring to bear.
d.x: He considered exerting his influence on John to gain an advantage for himself.

d.g: To put in vigorous action.
d.x: I exerted myself in today's training.

exert.e: From Latin exsertus, past participle of exserō (“to stretch or thrust forth or out”), from ex- + serō (“to string together”).

d.g: To remove the leaves from a plant.
To remove a layer of dead skin cells, as in cosmetic preparation.
To split into scales, especially to become converted into scales as the result of heat or decomposition.

exfoliate.e: From Late Latin exfoliō (“to strip of leaves”), from ex- (“out of”) + folium (“leaf”); compare effoliate and French exfolier.

d.g: To expel air from the lungs through the nose or mouth by action of the diaphragm, to breathe out.
To expel (something, such as tobacco smoke) from the lungs by action of the diaphragm.
To pass off in the form of vapour; to emerge.
d.x: Above was a tiled roof – though from that imperfect tiling exhaled stench and pestilence.

d.g: To emit (a vapour, an odour, etc.).
d.x: The earth exhales vapor; marshes exhale noxious effluvia.

exhale.e: From Middle French exhaler, from Latin exhalare, from ex (“out”) + halare (“to breathe”).

d.g: To cheer, to cheer up, to gladden, to make happy, to elate.
d.x: Good news exhilarates the mind; wine exhilarates the drinker.

d.g: To excite, to thrill.

exhilarate.e: From Latin exhilarō (“to delight, to gladden, to make merry”), from ex- (“out, away”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out”)) + hilarō (“to cheer, to gladden”), from hilaris (“cheerful, light-hearted, lively”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, merry”), from ἵλαος (hílaos, “gracious, kind, propitious”), …

d.g: To urge; to advise earnestly.
d.x: And with many other words did hee testifie and exhort, saying, Saue your selues from this vntoward generation.

exhort.e: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

d.g: To dig out of the ground; to take out of a place of burial; to disinter.
d.x: The archeologist exhumed artifacts from the ground with a shovel.

d.g: To uncover; to bring to light.
d.x: Long dead traditions are exhumed just for the tourists.

exhume.e: From Medieval Latin exhumō, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).

d.g: to be; have existence; have being or reality

exist.e: From French exister, from Latin existō, exsistō (“I am, I exist, appear, arise”), from ex (“out”) + sistere (“to set, place”) (related to stare (“to stand, to be stood”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from the root *steh₂- (“stand”); see stand. …

d.g: To free (someone) from an obligation, responsibility or task.
To free (someone) from accusation or blame.

exonerate.e: From Middle English exoneraten (attested in past participle exonerated), from Latin exonerātus, past perfect participle of exonerō (“to discharge, unload; to exonerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). …

d.g: To drive out (an evil spirit) from a person, place or thing, especially by an incantation or prayer.
d.x: The priest attempted to exorcise the evil spirit from the house.

d.g: To rid (a person, place or thing) of an evil spirit.
d.x: They hired a specialist to exorcise the haunted object.

exorcise.e: From Middle English exorcisen, exorzisen, from Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos). Compare Old French exorciser.

d.g: US spelling of exorcise.
To change (something) from a smaller form or size to a larger one; to spread out or lay open.
d.x: You can expand this compact umbrella to cover a large table.

d.g: To increase the extent, number, volume or scope of (something).
d.x: A flower expands its leaves.

d.g: To express (something) at length and/or in detail.
To rewrite (an expression) as a longer, yet equivalent, sum of terms.
d.x: Use the binomial theorem to expand #123;(x#43;1)#125;⁴.

expand.e: Recorded in Middle English since 1422 (as expanden, expaunden), from Anglo-Norman espaundre, from Latin expandere (“to spread out”), itself from ex- (“out, outwards”) + pandō (“to spread”). Doublet of spawn.

d.g: To write or speak at length; to be copious in argument or discussion.
d.x: Now, as the business of standing mast-heads, ashore or afloat, is a very ancient and interesting one, let us in some measure expatiate here.

d.g: To range at large, or without restraint.

expatiate.e: From the participle stem of Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior (“walk about”).

d.g: To predict or believe that something will happen
d.x: when you least expect it

d.g: To consider obligatory or required.
d.x: England expects that every man will do his duty.

d.g: To consider reasonably due.
d.x: My parents expected too much of me when I was in college.

d.g: To be pregnant, to consider a baby due.
d.x: We are expecting our third in June.

expect.e: From Latin expectāre, infinitive form of exspectō (“look out for, await, expect”), from ex (“out”) + spectō (“look at”), frequentative of speciō (“see”).

d.g: To cough up fluid from the lungs.
d.x: …the gap in his upper row of teeth enabled him to expectorate in a new and admirable way.

d.g: To spit.

expectorate.e: From Latin expectorātus, past participle of expectorō (“(only figurative) banish from the mind; (post-classical) expel from the breast)”), from ex (“out of”) + pectus (“the breast”).

d.g: To accelerate the progress of.
d.x: He expedited the search by alphabetizing the papers.

d.g: To perform (a task) fast and efficiently.
To perform the duties of an expediter.
Free of impediment; unimpeded.
d.x: […] to make the way plaine and expedite […]

expedite.e: From Latin expedītus (“unimpeded, unfettered”), perfect passive participle of expediō (“bring forward, set right”).

d.g: To eject.
To remove from membership.
d.x: He was expelled from school multiple times for disruptive behaviour.

d.g: To deport.

expel.e: Late Middle English: from Latin expellere, from ex- (“out”) + pellere (“to drive”).

d.g: To consume, exhaust (some resource).
d.x:
If my death might make this island happy […]
I would expend it with all willingness.

expend.e: Borrowed from Latin expendō (“to weigh; to pay out”). Doublet of spend.

d.g: To atone or make reparation for.
d.x: The Treasurer obliged himself to expiate the injury.

d.g: To make amends or pay the penalty for.
d.x: He had only to live and expiate in solitude the crimes which he had committed.

d.g: To purify with sacred rites.
To wind up, bring to an end.
d.x: But when in thee times forrwes I behould, / Then look I death my daies ſhould expiate.

expiate.e: From Latin expiātus, past participle of expiō (“atone for”).

d.g: To die.
d.x: The patient expired in hospital.

d.g: To lapse and become invalid.
d.x: My library card will expire next week.

d.g: To come to an end; to conclude.
d.x: And when the thousand yeeres are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, […]

d.g: To exhale; to breathe out.
d.x: Anatomy exhibits the lungs in a continual motion of inspiring and expiring air.

expire.e: From Middle English expire, from Middle French expirer, from Latin expīrō, exspīrō, from ex- (“out”) + spīrō (“breathe, be alive”).

d.g: To clarify and make something plain or intelligible.
d.x: The issue was explained to the governor in detail.

d.g: To give the reason for, justification for, or cause of.

explain.e: From Middle English explanen, from Old French explaner, from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”), from ex- (“out”) + planō (“to flatten, make level”), from planus (“level, plain”); see plain and plane. Compare esplanade, splanade. Displaced Old English reċċan.

d.g: To explain meticulously or in great detail.
d.x: My homework is to explicate a poem.

d.g: To fly apart with sudden violent force; to blow up, to burst, to detonate, to go off.
d.x: The bomb explodes.

d.g: To destroy with an explosion.
d.x: The assassin exploded the car by means of a car bomb.

d.g: To make a violent or emotional outburst; to suddenly give expression to powerful and often negative or unpleasant emotion, especially anger.
d.x: She exploded when I criticised her hat.

d.g: To increase suddenly.
d.x: When pigeons can come to a spot day in and day out for a guaranteed meal, their populations explode.

d.g: To ejaculate.

explode.e: First recorded around 1538, from the Latin verb explōdere (“drive out or off by clapping”). The meaning was originally theatrical, "to drive an actor off the stage by making noise," hence meaning to "to drive out" or "to reject". From ex- (“out”) + plaudere (“to clap; to applaud”). …

d.g: To examine or investigate something systematically.
d.x: The committee has been exploring alternative solutions to the problem at hand.

d.g: To travel somewhere in search of discovery.
d.x: It was around that time that the expedition began exploring the Arctic Circle.
